list.listitem: Diagnosis of alopecia is based on history and physical findings; in unclear cases or when scarring alopecia is suspected, a skin biopsy is recommended. C
Minoxidil 5% topical solution (preferred initial therapy for men and women) and oral finasteride 1mg daily (FDA approved for men only) are treatment options for androgenetic alopecia. A
Patients with alopecia areata and less than 50% scalp involvement also benefit from intralesional corticosteroid injections. B
Topical immunotherapy with diphenylcyclopropenone may be effective for extensive alopecia areata. B
Oral janus kinase inhibitors baricitinib, A deuruxolitinib and ritlecitinib B are options for severe alopecia areata although their long-term safety is uncertain.

background.definition: Alopecia is defined as hair loss, typically involving the scalp but may involve any hair-bearing skin. Alopecias are generally classified as nonscarring (noncicatricial) and scarring (cicatricial). Nonscarring alopecia usually does not lead to destruction of the hair unit, whereas scarring alopecia leads to permanent, irreversible loss of hair. However, in later stages of some nonscarring alopecias, permanent hair loss can also occur.

list.listitem: Androgenetic alopecia eventually occurs in approximately 60% to 80% of white men; approximately 20% of white men will have some alopecia starting shortly after puberty. The prevalence increases by decade of life so that 30% of men in their 30s will have alopecia and 50% of men will have some evidence of alopecia by the age of 50 years.
Black men develop alopecia at approximately one-fourth the rate of white men.
Japanese men also are much less likely to develop alopecia.
Alopecia in Chinese men is unusual before the age of 40 years.
Women also develop androgenetic alopecia, although less frequently and later in life. Approximately 40% of women older than 70 years of age will develop alopecia.
The incidence of alopecia areata is 0.2 per 1000 persons per year in a Minnesota general population study.
A total of 97% of patients in one series with central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA) were women and most were of African descent.
Hair loss may cause significant emotional problems, especially in young women and children. Clinical severity of hair loss does not necessarily predict impact on quality of life.
Patients with alopecia areata have poor health-related quality of life scores, similar to those seen in patients with other skin diseases such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.
Hair loss is the reason for 3% of pediatrician visits each year in the United States.

Nonscarring alopecias include androgenetic alopecia [which encompass male pattern hair loss (MPHL) and female pattern hair loss (FPHL)], telogen effluvium, alopecia areata (AA), tinea capitis, traction alopecia, and trichotillomania. Despite their classification as nonscarring alopecias, permanent hair loss or scarring is seen during advanced stages of androgenetic alopecia, AA, traction alopecia, and tinea capitis.

Scarring alopecias include discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) of the scalp, two variants of lichen planus called lichen planopilaris (LPP) and frontal fibrosing alopecia (FFA), central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), acne keloidalis nuchae, folliculitis decalvans, and dissecting cellulitis of the scalp.

Androgenetic alopecia is the most common cause of baldness in men and women. The roles of androgens and genetics are more established in MPHL than in FPHL. Without intervention, both disorders lead to slow, progressive loss and thinning of hair.
Telogen effluvium occurs when there is an increase in the percentage of hairs in the telogen (resting) phase. This may occur after periods of stress, such as pregnancy or a major illness.

Alopecia areata (AA) involves an autoimmune component in which the immune system attacks the follicles, resulting in hair loss. The areas of hair loss are frequently round with very soft scalp skin that remains. Alopecia totalis is defined by total loss of scalp hair. Alopecia universalis occurs when all hairs from head to toe are lost.

AA and tinea capitis are the most common causes of alopecia in children. In the U.S., Western Europe and Central America, tinea capitis caused by Trichophyton is most prevalent, whereas Mircrosporum species are predominant in South America, Central and Southern Europe, Western Asia, and Africa.

Traumatic alopecias include traction alopecia and trichotillomania. Traction alopecia occurs from the chronic pulling of hair generally related to hairstyles with braids. Trichotillomania is a condition in which the person pulls out hairs often because of some type of psychological disturbance.
Radiation therapy for cancer treatment can damage hair follicles and lead to hair loss. Likewise, chemotherapy may induce alopecia.
DLE is a scarring alopecia in which visible scalp changes include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, and atrophy. It is a localized form of cutaneous lupus.
LPP is a type of scarring alopecia in which there is follicular plugging and a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate. The person does not need to have lichen planus of the skin to have this condition.

CCCA is characterized by central scalp hair loss. It is most common in women of African descent, may have genetic associations, and may be aggravated by traumatic hair care practices and hair chemicals.
Acne keloidalis nuchae presents with papules, pustules, and nodules at and above the posterior nuchal hairline and can lead to hair loss in that region.
Folliculitis decalvans is a scarring alopecia with pustules in a predominantly neutrophilic infiltrate. The pustular regions often grow out Staphylococcus aureus.

Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp is a scarring alopecia with purulent discharge, sinus tracts, and visible scarring. It may be part of the follicular occlusion triad as seen with hidradenitis suppurativa and severe inflammatory acne.

Hair follicles continually go through three phases: anagen, catagen, and telogen (growth, involution, and resting, respectively). In androgenetic alopecia, the follicle is normal but the hair growth cycling is abnormal. In cicatricial and traumatic alopecias, the hair follicle itself is damaged.
Androgenetic alopecia is due to a genetically determined shortening of the anagen phase.
AA is an autoimmune disease thought to be mediated by autoreactive T lymphocytes.
Telogen effluvium occurs when a triggering condition, like childbirth or severe illness, causes the follicles to move to a telogen rather than anagen-predominant distribution.

Scarring alopecias occur when there is inflammation and destruction of the hair follicles leading to fibrous tissue formation. Scarring alopecias are further divided between lymphocytic and neutrophilic cicatricial alopecias, based on the predominant inflammatory infiltrate on histopathologic exam. Lymphocytic cicatricial alopecias include DLE, LPP, FFA, and CCCA. Neutrophilic cicatricial alopecias include folliculitis decalvans and dissecting cellulitis. Acne keloidalis nuchae has a mixed-cell infiltrate.
Consider the diagnosis of androgenetic alopecia in men with gradual hair loss along the frontotemporal scalp and in women with progressive hair thinning at the crown and vertex scalp. C
Suspect telogen effluvium in patients with diffuse shedding of hair months after childbirth, severe illness, or major surgery, and a positive hair pull test during active disease. C
Patchy hair loss may be seen in alopecia areata, tinea capitis, trichotillomania, and discoid lupus erythematosus. C
Traction alopecia should be suspected in patients with alopecia along areas of the scalp subjected to chronic hair traction, such as weaves, tight braids, and ponytails. C
Consider performing scalp biopsy in cases of clinical uncertainty, especially when scarring alopecia is suspected. Early diagnosis and intervention may alter the course of scarring alopecias. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Tendency to maintain frontal hairline; diffuse thinning occurs at the crown and vertex scalp
Hair loss occurs in a typical M-shaped pattern in the frontal hairline
Smooth circular areas of hair loss; "exclamation point" hairs characteristic; pitting of nails
Typically related to stressful event like childbirth, severe illness and surgery; drugs and endocrinopathies may also be causative factors

Scarring is present in the scalp but is not always visible with the naked eye; biopsy is needed for diagnosis. Scarring alopecias may cause polytrichia, in which multiple hairs are seen emanating from a single follicle
Broken hairs remain firmly anchored in the scalp; hair loss is incomplete

list.listitem: Androgenetic alopecia has a gradual onset; abrupt onset suggests either telogen effluvium or alopecia areata.
Onset prior to puberty is unlikely to be androgenetic alopecia or telogen effluvium.
Approximately 20% of patients with alopecia areata have a positive family history.

A history of a stressful event or childbirth within the previous 2 to 4 months may be suggestive of telogen effluvium. A study of 823 women complaining of hair loss found that telogen effluvium related hair shedding was most common in October and November, with a secondary peak in June and July.
Acne keloidalis nuchae includes a history of short haircuts or scalp shaving that has worsened the condition.
Dissecting folliculitis often includes a history of severe inflammatory acne on the face and/or trunk along with a history of hidradenitis.

Patients noticing hair loss may appear to have a full head of hair, as up to 20% of hair may be lost before the loss is cosmetically apparent. In the "pull test," approximately 60 hairs are grasped between thumb, index finger, and middle fingers from the base near the scalp, and pulled firmly, but not forcefully, away from the scalp. If more than 2 hairs are obtained, this constitutes a positive pull test and implies active hair shedding; 2 hairs or fewer is considered normal physiologic shedding. Patients do not have to refrain from shampooing or brushing hair prior to the pull test.

The pattern of hair loss can indicate the cause. Male pattern hair loss suggests androgenetic alopecia, whereas hair loss at the temples may indicate traction alopecia. Alopecia at one area of the scalp may be a clue for trichotillomania.
The "fringe sign," the presence of retained hairs along the frontal and/or temporal rim, is a sensitive and specific clinical feature of traction alopecia.
Patchy hair loss without scarring is indicative of alopecia areata, whereas scarring patchy hair loss may be due to tinea capitis.
Establishing whether hair is broken off or shed at the roots may help determine the diagnosis.
Pitted nails and punctate lens opacities are frequently present in patients with alopecia areata.
Some women with androgenetic alopecia may have signs of androgen excess such as hirsutism and acne.
Multiple hairs emanating from a single follicle is highly suggestive of a scarring alopecia.
Look for scalp changes including hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, and atrophy as these may indicate discoid lupus erythematosus.
Lichen planopilaris involves follicular plugging.
Folliculitis decalvans includes pustules with polytrichia and visible scalp scarring.
Sinus tracts and visible scarring are seen in dissecting folliculitis.
Examine axillary and inguinal areas for hidradenitis and look for acne scarring on the face and trunk.

If tinea capitis is on the differential diagnosis, perform a scraping of the involved area including scale and broken hair. Start with a KOH preparation and if the results are negative consider sending a specimen for fungal culture. Unless the clinician has expertise with KOH preparations there is a high risk of false negative results.
Serum ferritin may be useful in women with hair loss, as low levels appear to be significantly linked to the presence of excessive hair loss.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) testing may be helpful in patients with a hair loss pattern and other signs and symptoms suggestive of thyroid dysfunction.
In women with clinical evidence of androgen excess, obtain free testosterone and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate levels.
Consider serology for syphilis and lupus erythematosus when diagnosis is in doubt.
Perform two 4-mm punch biopsies when scarring alopecia is suspected. The pathologist should cut one specimen vertically and the other horizontally to maximize the information for diagnosis.

A third 4-mm punch biopsy for direct immunofluorescence may be helpful for diagnosis of lupus erythematosus in histopathologically inconclusive cases. It is also valuable if bullous disease is suspected.
Video dermatoscopy may be useful where available as a noninvasive diagnostic tool, although further studies are needed to establish accuracy. This requires a dermatoscope and specialized training.
Dermoscopy can be used for diagnosis and grading criteria for androgenetic alopecia.

The cause of alopecia can be determined by ascertaining the abruptness of onset and duration, the circumstances (medication use, illness, or trauma), the pattern of hair loss, and qualities of the hair.
See for differential diagnoses.

For selected patients, testing the TSH, ferritin, and free testosterone; taking a fungal culture; and testing for syphilis and systemic lupus erythematosus may be helpful if relevant conditions are clinically suspected.
Topical minoxidil 5% and 2% twice daily are effective treatments for androgenetic alopecia in men and women. A

Oral finasteride 1mg daily and oral dutasteride 0.5mg daily appear to improve hair counts in men with androgenetic alopecia, but their use leads to more sexual side effects. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors do not appear to be beneficial for women. A
Intralesional corticosteroid injections lead to hair regrowth in patients with alopecia areata. B
Topical immunotherapy with diphenylcyclopropenone may be effective for extensive alopecia areata. B
Oral janus kinase inhibitors baricitinib, A deuruxolitinib and ritlecitinib B are options for severe alopecia areata although their long-term safety is uncertain.

The preferred treatment for androgenetic alopecia is topical minoxidil. Minoxidil 5% twice daily may result in greater hair counts than 2% administered twice a day in men. Based on systematic reviews, topical minoxidil 2% and 5% applied twice daily are effective for FPHL. Side effects include local irritation and hypertrichosis. Treatment is continued indefinitely; hair regrowth is lost if treatment is stopped.
In one RCT, topical minoxidil 5% plus topical tretinoin 0.01% once daily in men with MPHL showed similar efficacy as topical minoxidil 5% twice daily.

A small Brazilian study of 90 men showed similar efficacy of oral minoxidil 5 mg daily and topical minoxidil 5% twice daily. Oral minoxidil was significantly more effective on measurement of terminal hair density at the vertex, otherwise similar outcomes were noted.

A meta-analysis comparing oral and topical minoxidil solution in patients with AGA demonstrated similar efficacy and safety, with equivalent improvements in hair density, hair diameter, and incidence of adverse events, such as hypotension.

5-alpha-reductase inhibitors can be used in men with androgenetic alopecia. Oral finasteride 1 mg per day improves scalp coverage in approximately two-thirds of men. It has been shown in a systematic review to lead to higher hair counts than topical minoxidil. However, finasteride does not appear to be effective for women. A systematic review of 12 studies with 3927 patients concluded that finasteride was effective, with NNT of 6 for self-perceived short-term improvement and 3.4 for long-term improvement in hair coverage. However, there was an increased risk of erectile dysfunction with finasteride, although the absolute risk was low (NNH = 82).

A twin study of dutasteride showed that it significantly reduced hair loss progression in men with androgenetic alopecia. A Korean study, where dutasteride is approved for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia, showed improved hair growth in men treated with dutasteride 0.5 mg. Another RCT demonstrated that dutasteride 0.5 mg was superior to 1 mg finasteride, and finasteride was superior to placebo in increasing hair count and width after 24 weeks in male patients with MPHL. The rate of sexual adverse effects was similar for both active treatment groups, but lower in the placebo group. Dutasteride is not FDA-approved for the treatment of androgenetic alopecia. A systematic review also found dutasteride to have better efficacy than finasteride for MPHL, with similar adverse effects.
Oral or topical hormonal therapy (cyproterone acetate, flutamide, spironolactone, drosperinone) is not recommended for women as a treatment for hair loss.

A meta-analysis of topical prostaglandin analogs including bimatoprost, latanaprost and cetirizine, concluded that these agents promote superior hair growth in all included studies compared to controls. This meta-analysis included hair loss on scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes due to various causes including chemotherapy, AGA and AA among others. Given the small scale of the included studies, further research is needed to determine optimal dose and duration of treatment.

Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections appear to improve hair density and diameter in small studies in men and women with androgenetic alopecia. However, pooled results from a 2017 meta-analysis of six small studies did not show statistical significance for increases in hair number and hair thickness. A later meta-analysis of ten small studies concluded PRP treatment increases hair density in patients with androgenetic alopecia. Monthly injections for 3 months are recommended followed by maintenance injection after three to six months.
A study in adults with trichotillomania found that N-acetylcysteine (1200 mg per day) was effective over a 6-week study period with a NNT of 2.0.

However, a 2021 Cochrane review found inconclusive evidence for the effectiveness of any specific pharmacologic treatment for trichotillomania. Four small trials provided limited evidence for the efficacy of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), clomipramine, and olanzapine.
Alopecia Areata (AA)

British Academy of Dermatology guidelines recommend beginning with a potent or very potent topic corticosteroid once daily or intralesional triamcinolone as first-line treatments for alopecia areata. Consider oral steroids for patients with rapidly progressive AA. For patients with moderate to severe AA consider methotrexate (MTX) as monotherapy or in combination with oral corticosteroids.

A 2023 Cochrane review that evaluated therapies for alopecia areata, which included 63 trials with 4817 randomized participants, found that treatment with baricitinib results in an increase in short‐ and long‐term hair regrowth compared to placebo, and that the impact of other treatments on hair regrowth is uncertain.

In patients with alopecia areata with less than 50% scalp involvement, intralesional injection with triamcinolone appear to be effective based on a systematic review of 3 RCTs and 3 obsevational studies. A dose of 5 mg/ml appears to be optimal in terms of efficacy and adverse events. A dose of < 5 mg/ml was significantly less effective, while a dose of 10 mg/ml was no more effective and had more adverse effects.

A systematic review of retrospective observational trials showed that methotrexate (MTX) may be an effective treatment for severe alopecia areata. There appears to be a higher response rate in patients treated with MTX and corticosteroids in combination, however recurrence was common with tapering therapy and data on long term effectiveness is limited.

A trial randomized 89 patients with alopecia totalis/universalis to methotrexate 25 mg/week or placebo for 6 months. Those with a response at 6 months continued their therapy for another 6 months. Those without a response were rerandomized to MTX + prednisone 20 mg/day or MTX + placebo for 6 months. Complete or almost complete hair regrowth was seen in no patients who received placebo alone, 1 patient who received MTX alone, 7 of 35 (20%) who got MTX + prednisone, and 5 of 16 who get MTX for 6 months followed by prednisone for 6 months. This trial provides some support for adding prednisone 20 mg/day (tapering to 15 mg/day after 3 months) for patients in whom MTX alone is ineffective.
Topical immunotherapy with diphenylcyclopropenone may be effective for a small group of patients with extensive alopecia areata.

A systematic review of contact immunotherapy for severe alopecia areata showed the rate of any hair regrowth was 65% among patients treated with contact immunotherapy, while complete regrowth rate was 32%. Recurrence rates were 38% in patients receiving maintenance treatment and 49% in patients not receiving maintenance treatment.

Oral janus kinase inhibitors are effective for severe alopecia areata. Baricitinib for 36 weeks resulted in 39% of patients taking 4 mg daily having improvement in SALT score to 20 or less compared to 23% of patients taking 2 mg daily and 6% of patients in the placebo group (NNT = 3 and 6 respectively).
A trial identified non-responders to baricitinib 2 mg and after failure to adequately respond after a year uptitrated them to 4 mg. About a quarter responded favorably.

Adults with at least 50% hair loss from alopecia areata who took deuruxolitinib for 24 weeks achieved equal to or less than 20% hair loss significantly more often than those who took a placebo (NNT = 2.6 and 3.8 for the 12 mg and 8 mg daily doses, respectively).
A patient with androgenetic alopecia may choose hair transplantation. There are few studies on the efficacy of hair transplantation in men or women.
Topical garlic gel may be an effective adjunct to topical betamethasone valerate in treating alopecia areata.
Aromatherapy may be of some benefit for patients with alopecia areata.
An evidence-based guideline found little evidence for complementary therapies for androgenetic alopecia.

A systematic review identified 16 studies of CAM therapies for alopecia areata, including 5 RCTs. They found the best (albeit low quality) evidence for essential oil aromatherapy, topical garlic, and oral glucosides of peony with compount glycyrrhizin.
Photobiomodulation (formerly known as low-level laser light therapy) may promote hair regrowth in patients with androgenetic alopecia.
Telogen effluvium typically resolves spontaneously; patient reassurance is very important.
Emotional disturbance is common, especially in patients with extensive hair loss. Psychological treatment may be necessary.
Wigs may help ameliorate the psychological impact of extensive hair loss.
Scalp cooling device use in women undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer significantly decreases hair loss measured after the fourth treatment cycle.

Referral to a dermatologist is needed for all the scarring alopecias and refractory cases of alopecia areata. Cases of alopecia totalis and alopecia universalis should be referred early to a dermatologist.
Up to 80% of patients with limited alopecia areata for less than 1 year will experience spontaneous regrowth of hair. B

The prognosis in alopecia areata is less favorable when onset is in early childhood, the patient has severe disease, duration is more than 1 year, there is ophiasis (involvement of the peripheral scalp), and there is concurrent history of atopy. It is better when regenerated vellus hairs are present.B
Patchy alopecia patients with a positive family history of alopecia areata have reduced hair regrowth after relapses. C
Alopecia areata is associated with several systemic diseases including autoimmune thyroid disease, metabolic syndrome, iron deficiency anemia, vitamin D deficiency, and psychiatric disorders. B
The prognosis for hair regrowth in all cases of scarring alopecia is poor. C
Pregnancy may cause either an increase or a decrease in hair growth. Thickening of scalp hair may be noted due to prolonged anagen phase.
The hair enters a prolonged telogen phase postpartum, sometimes causing telogen effluvium for up to 1 year.
Treatment of hair loss is limited in pregnancy due to potential toxicities of corticosteroids and minoxidil. Cosmetic treatments such as wigs may be a reasonable option until the pregnancy is over.
Peak incidence occurs in young children 0 to 6 years of age.
The approach to diagnosis is similar to that in adults, and treatment approaches are similar to those for adults, although intralesional corticosteroids may not be well tolerated.

Children with trichotillomania may be amenable to behavioral interventions as they are frequently not aware that they are plucking their hair. An RCT in adults found that N-acetylcysteine was effective for this condition, but it has not been evaluated for safety and efficacy in children. A clinical trial is underway (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00993265).

cell.label: History and physical examination: scarring present or absent?
Hereditary disorders; trauma: mechanical, burns, caustic agents, radiation; or systemic disease: discoid lupus, sarcoidosis, lichen planus, necrobiosis lipoidica, others
Infection (fungal, bacterial, protozoan); or neoplasm: basal cell carcinoma (morpheaform), squamous cell carcinoma, metastatic carcinoma (alopecia neoplastica), lymphoma, or adnexal tumors
Total testosterone, free testosterone, DHEA-S, prolactin levels
Thyroid function tests to rule out thyroid disease VDRL test to rule out syphilis Ferritin level to rule out iron deficiency ANA test to rule out systemic lupus erythematosus

Laboratory results normal; consider: other nutritional deficiency (malnutrition, sprue, zinc deficiency) Telogen effluvium Trauma (trichotillomania, traction alopecia) Hereditary syndromes Alopecia areata Androgenetic alopecia

footnotes.footnote: *Clinical signs and symptoms of androgen excess include menstrual irregularities, infertility, hirsutism, severe cystic acne, virilization, and galactorrhea.
